utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you all hear me? The interpreters are ready? Can The Prosecutors hear me, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Registrar, you can hear me? No problems. So the judges hear me and the interpreters are ready? Good. Registrar, could you please introduce the case for the hearing today?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is case IT-95-13-1, Prosecutor against Mile Mrk{i}, Miroslav Radi} and Veselin [ljivan}anin. Who is representing the Prosecutor's office, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann. I appear with my co-counsel Mr. Williamson and I am assisted at the Bar table by Miss Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Prosecutor, before you begin the floor, I would like to reiterate for all those who are following our hearings that this is an International Tribunal. This is a hearing under Rule 61, under which an arrest warrant has not been executed for reasons that The Prosecutor is to outline -- indeed, he has already outlined and he is confirming to the Chamber, which is to sit as it now is sitting to hear the relevant evidence on the part of the Prosecution where witnesses or victims may be called. If the Chamber is convinced, of course, it may subsequently issue an international arrest warrant and may, via the President of the Tribunal, report to the Security Council the non-execution. So this is why we are presently sitting in respect of the case just announced by the Registrar. I am going to give you the floor, Prosecutor. I would like, first, to know whether any specific measures are going to be taken in so far as you have asked that witnesses be called. Prosecuting counsel, you have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Just to answer that first question, yes, an application has been filed. I understand an order has been given in relation to witnesses who we will -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have the microphone on, your Honour. Yes. An application has been made in relation to two witnesses who will be respectively referred to in the course of proceedings as A and B, but we will elaborate on that further, if your Honour pleases, when it comes to actually presenting their evidence. There is one matter, a preliminary matter, that I would like to raise in relation to the indictment itself before I commence my opening address. On page 4 of the indictment there is among a large list of names that appears there the name Goran Edelinski. In fact, it is Edelinski Goran. It is about the centre of the page and it has against that a reference to the date of birth, 29.7.75. Your Honour, that name we have subsequently discovered is in error and we would ask that, pursuant to Rule 50, with leave of the Chamber, that name be deleted from the list as an amendment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why? Is that an error or it is an error or why are you asking for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it is an error, your Honour. We have discovered that man was not at the place alleged at the time. We have now found that out to be the case and we ask that that be removed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am afraid, Prosecuting counsel, that is on page 4 -- we have got the French version, of course -- you have said towards the middle -- maybe the Registrar could point that out to me, if he could be so good?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is right in the middle of the page; I will spell the name out, E-D-E-L-I-N-S-K-I.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. OK. Fine. In the French version it is at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Registrar. Prosecuting counsel, if you would be so good, please, to go on with regard to the substantive aspects of the matter, and please tell us also how you are going to be presenting your evidence. I assume you are going to begin with a preliminary explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that was my intention. Your Honours, the indictments that you have before you for reconfirmation pursuant to Rule 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence charges Mile Mrk{i}, Miroslav Tadic and Veselin Veselin [ljivan}anin with Grave Breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Violations of the Laws and Customs of War, and Crimes Against Humanity. This technical legal terminology expressed in less formal terms means beatings and murder. The indictment is, therefore, concerned with the beating and murder of approximately 260 men and boys at Ovcara near Vukovar in Croatia on 20th November 1991. The motive for these murders was hatred based on ignorance, prejudice and intolerance. There was no justification for this crime. These men were not actively involved in armed conflict at the time of their death, They had committed no crime. Some of them may have held different political views to their executioners, some of them may have taken up arms in self-defence, but these are not crimes, at least crimes justifying their summary execution. The sole basis for the selection and their execution was the fact that they were a different national ethnic and political group, namely that they were Croatian. Where and under what circumstances did this happen? If the court pleases, Vukovar is located in the Eastern Slavonia region of Croatian on the banks of the Danube River, which marks the borders between Croatia and the Federal Republic of the former Yugoslavia (Vojvodina region of Serbia). The city straddles the Vuka river which flows into the Danube just north of the city centre. Southeast of the Vukovar the terrain consists mostly of 20 rolling hills and bluffs along the Danube rising up to the 21 Fruska Gora mountain 20 miles to the south-east. North of the Vuka, the terrain is very flat, as it is to the south and west. The area is primarily agricultural and most of the land is cultivated. There are relatively few forested areas. In the 1991 census, the city of Vukovar had a population of just over 44,000, consisting of 21,000 Croats, 14,500 Serbs, 4,300 Yugoslavs and 4,500 others. The Vukovar municipality op{tina which included the city and surrounding villages, then had a population of just over 84,000, of which 36,900 were Croat, 31,400 were Serb, 1,300 Hungarian, 6,100 Yugoslavs and 8,300 of other nationalities. The area to the north and west of Vukovar were predominantly Serb, while to south and east, the villages were mainly Croatian. In 1991, Vukovar was an affluent town in Croatia, due primarily to its position as the service centre for the surrounding agricultural areas, reputed to be the richest farmland in all of the former Yugoslavia. The regional economy was also supplemented by nearby oil and natural gas deposits, as well as by a large Borovo factory which employed almost 30,000 employees and manufactured shoes, leather and rubber products. Throughout its history, Vukovar has been a part of Croatia. During World War II, the region around Vukovar was relatively peaceful and it seems to have escaped much of the internecine ethnic fighting which occurred in other 18 areas of Yugoslavia. After the war, however, the significant ethnic German population was forced from the region by the Tito government, leading to an influx of settlers from other areas of Yugoslavia. Some of the newcomers were forcibly sent to Eastern Slavonia, but most apparently came on their own volition from the poor areas of Krajina (primarily Serbian people) and from Herzegovina (primarily Croats). They were seeking the rich farmland for which the area was well known. The ethnic tension first manifested itself in the Vukovar region after the death of Tito. The atmosphere of tension was exacerbated by Serbian radicals and, to a lesser extent, Croatian radicals, who visited the area in 1990 calling for violent "responses" to the other side's "provocation". As a result of these Serbian calls to defend their brethren in Croatia from the arriving new Croat government, large numbers of ultra-nationalist Serbs began arriving in the area to significantly strengthen the Serb irregular forces. These units were armed and provided logistical support by the JNA. In response to the build up of obviously hostile elements, the Croats also dispatched significant numbers of volunteers, police and later the Croatian National Guard, referred to as the ZNG. On both sides, the introduction of more and more well-armed ultra-nationalists and nationalists caused the situation to deteriorate even further. In April 1991, several Serb villages near Vukovar erected barricades at the entrance to the towns. The road blocks were manned by heavily armed individuals who restricted non-Serbs from travelling into or through the villages. It was at one of these road blocks in Borovo Selo (the largest town in Vukovar municipality) that two Croatian policemen were detained on the night of 1st May 1991. The following day, approximately 30 Croatian policemen in riot gear were sent to Borovo Selo to retrieve the captured officers. When they exited their buses they were fired on from an unknown number of Serbs who were waiting in ambush near the village Community Centre. 12 Croatian policemen were killed and almost all the others were wounded. This incident marked the beginning of armed conflict in the region, and from that point forward, there were gun battles occurring between the Serbs and Croats on an increasingly regular basis. These fights varied in intensity, but they usually ended with the arrival of the JNA units which "intervened" at this stage to separate the combatants. By mid-July, however, the JNA dropped the neutral stance that it had previously taken and began to side with the Serbs. The shift in the JNA position in Vukovar became obvious through a few relatively minor events such as a JNA tank destroying a Croatian police car on 8th July 1991, two JNA air attacks on the National Guard positions on 13th and 22nd July, a tank attack on a police training facility on 25th July. As these incidents were occurring, the JNA steadily increased its presence in the Vukovar area. By mid-August, the JNA had deployed troops in the Croatian side of the Danube in such a manner as to almost entirely encircle the city of Vukovar. Also, the JNA placed additional units on the Serbian side of the river and there they erected a number of artillery and rocket emplacements. These forces were also supplemented by at least three gunboats from the Danube River which were deployed in the river above the town. On 25th August 1991, the JNA launched a full scale assault on Vukovar. For the first time land, air and naval forces were all utilized in a co-ordinated attack, further supported by Serb irregular forces. Reportedly, thousands of rockets and artillery shells were fired on the city, and a number of bombs were dropped from JNA aircraft. The bombardment caused extensive damage, particularly to the hospital, the city water tower, the radio transmitter, and also to several of the churches. Simultaneous to this, the JNA launched an armoured assault, using tanks and APCs, but with relatively little infantry support. The land attack was repelled without any substantial gains by the JNA, but the army was able to further constrict Vukovar by cutting telephone lines linking the city to the outside world. When the attacks tapered off three days later, the road to Vinkovci had been cut by the JNA, so the Croats were left only with an improvised track through cornfields as their sole supply and communication link. On the Croatian side there were approximately 1800 men who had been loosely formed into volunteer defence force for the city. At first this force was poorly organised and contained few professional soldiers. However, in time it organised itself into a much more effective unit within the structure of an infantry brigade with a clear chain of command and with designated areas of responsibility. The core of the Croat forces had initially been policemen from the Croatian Ministry of Interior, which was supplemented by local men, many of whom had previously served their obligatory term with the JNA as conscripts. As tension had risen in the area, a few units from the ZNG (Croatian National Guard) had also joined the force. Initially, the defenders maintained a defence line of some 36 kilometres encompassing most of the city and the nearby Croat suburb of Borovo Naselje. Although Croatian held territory outside this line had been taken by the JNA, the defence line itself largely held through the 25th August 1991 attack. Over the next three months, however, it was gradually pushed back as a result of continuous bombardment and repeated armoured assaults. Throughout the attack until the fall of the city, the JNA continued shelling the city unabated. On most days the bombardment of the city went on continuously 24 hours a day, usually without any discernible intervals between shots. Estimates from Croatian sources regularly place the number of rounds fired on the city as at least 2,500 a day and on some days up to as much as 16,000. Additional reliable reports state that JNA aircraft were flying an average of 50 sorties a day against the city, adding their bombs and missiles to the onslaught. Most of these bombardments occurred without any significant activity by the land forces. Once the JNA failed to gain ground initially, reinforcements were sent to the Vukovar theatre in increasing numbers. As more troops and weaponry arrived, the JNA engaged in several other large-scale attacks on the city, notable those commencing on 5th September through to 4th November 1991. Throughout this period, the bombardment campaign had substantially damaged most of the buildings in the city and had totally destroyed many. By the time of the 4th November attack was launched, few buildings in the Croatian areas of the town were left standing. The final offensive steadily progressed over a two-week period and finally resulted in cutting off the Croatian forces in Borovo Naselje from those in Vukovar proper on 15th November 1991. Three days later, the Croatian forces were further split when the units at Mitnica were cut off from the forces in the centre of the town. The remaining Croatian defenders then surrendered on 18 November 1991, though significant numbers of them were killed on the spot or were executed shortly thereafter. By the time the city fell, the JNA had amassed in excess of 30,000 troops in the Vukovar area. The vast majority of these troops were contributed by the 1st Military District (Belgrade), the Novi Sad Corps, the Tuzla Corps, the Kragujevac Corps, the Guards Mechanized Division, the Guards Brigade and the Danube River Flotilla. Additional units were also drawn from the 3rd Military District. These JNA forces were joined by significant numbers of Serbs irregular troops, coming from Territorial Defence Units as well as volunteers who had flocked to the area from Serbia, Montenegro and the Serbian regions of Croatia. The JNA/Serb forces apparently had at their disposal most of the weaponry in the JNA armoury. Rockets and artillery emplacements were sited on all sides of the city, and every type and standard JNA heavy weapon was utilized, including howitzers, mortars, battle tanks, armoured personnel carriers, naval gunboats from the River Danube flotilla and fighter/bomber aircraft. The JNA/Serb forces were overwhelmingly stronger than Croatian forces defending Vukovar. The attackers had at least 15:1 advantage in manpower, and their advantage in artillery and tanks was certainly greater than 100:1 ratio. Additionally, the JNA used aircraft and naval gunboats which were completely unavailable to the Croatians. Despite this overwhelming superiority, the battle of Vukovar lasted just short of three months. During the course of the battle, at least 50 per cent of the buildings in the city were totally destroyed. 90 per cent of the buildings in the city centre were destroyed. Another 40 per cent suffered substantial damage. At least 1,100 civilians died before the fall of the city, most of them as a result of the shelling. This number constituted over 10 per cent of the persons who had remained in Vukovar after the city was encircled. Another 350 soldiers were also killed during the course of the battle. Serb residential areas in the city were largely spared from the artillery, rocket and air attacks launched on the town. This, despite the fact that those areas too were behind the Croatian lines and Croatian soldiers were setting up defensive positions there as well. It appears that these areas were only hit when there was no other option to dislodge the Croats than to target those buildings. Other than the avoidance of predominantly Serb areas, everything else in the town was subject to attack. This included the hospital, churches and the town's museum. Generally, the capabilities of the Croats to inflict damage against the JNA forces was extremely limited. They certainly could not launch offensive operations of any kind, and the ammunition for their heavy weapons was carefully preserved for defensive use only. Indicative of this fact that the JNA barracks on the south side of Vukovar remained in the hands of the JNA throughout the whole course of the battle, and although it abutted the front-line, the facility sustained almost no damage. Throughout the course of the siege, the Vukovar Hospital kept functioning notwithstanding the fact that it too was constantly shelled. Head Doctor and Director of the Hospital, Dr. Bosanac, who will give evidence in these proceedings, maintained an heroic vigil contacting outside world and international organisations, informing the world of what was happening to Vukovar and especially to the hospital. She contacted the local barracks of the JNA and asked why they were being attacked by the Federal Army, but this was to no avail. The Vukovar Hospital is located in the centre of the city. The hospital was well sign-posted. On its roof was painted a large red cross sign and a big linen cross sign was displayed in the courtyard of the hospital, but rather than save the hospital from bombardment, including aerial bombardment, the hospital was constantly attacked as if the signs on the roof and in the yard were to be used as targets. Frantic efforts were made by the Director of the Hospital, Dr. Bosanac, to stop the shelling of the hospital, but her pleas fell on deaf ears. She was instrumental in planning for the sick and wounded of the hospital to be evacuated under the supervision of the European Community Monitoring Mission and the International Committee for the Red Cross. The fact that she involved both of these organisations was probably instrumental in the saving of the many lives. Word got out among the trapped community of Vukovar that this evacuation was to take place from the hospital under the supervision of ECMM and the ICRC - the supervised evacuation was to take place on 18th November 1991 from the hospital to free Croatia. Many hundreds of the townsfolk gathered at the hospital. Just as this evacuation was to commence, the accused, Major Veselin [ljivan}anin, a JNA officer, entered the hospital with his troops and assumed control. He ordered the nursing staff into a dressing room of the hospital on the pretext of calling a meeting. Meanwhile his troops under his command and control separated the men from the women. No regard was had for the fact that the majority of the men patients were sick or wounded. Assisted by paramilitary volunteers and profiteers, the JNA soldiers hurriedly removed about 300 men and boys from the hospital. There then followed a series of events which we have seen repeated again and again in the course of this terrible war. The repetition and similarity is so striking as to put aside altogether any suggestion of coincidence; so similar in detail that the only conclusion available is that it was part of some plan. The events that occurred in Vukovar was but the very beginning of what was later to become known as ethnic cleansing, thus planting the seeds of genocide in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. These unfortunate men were loaded into buses under the direct orders of Major Veselin [ljivan}anin. They were taken to Ovcara, a farm nearby the town, from where they were then forced to run the gauntlet between two lines of soldiers and paramilitaries who beat them as they passed. Inside the building on the farm the men were then beaten in an orgy of violence for a period of several hours. At least two men succumbed to the beatings and died. The prisoners were then loaded into trucks in groups of 10 to 20. They were then taken to their killing fields were a mass grave site had been prepared, and where they were systematically and brutally murdered. Approximately 260 men and boys were slaughtered that night. Some of the men were as young as 16 years of age, others were as old as 76. In the course of these proceedings the Prosecution will call some 11 witnesses. The first witness will be Dr. Gow. Dr. Gow will give an historical overview of prewar Yugoslavia. He will give evidence of the events that led up to the war between Serbia and Croatia in mid-1991. He will provide the evidence relating to the widespread and systematic nature of these crimes. The next witness will be an investigator from the Tribunal who will also provide an overview of the case from the point of view of the investigation. We will call evidence of a preliminary examinations that have been carried out by experts on the mass grave at Ovcara. We will call some evidence of eyewitnesses who were at the hospital during the course of the siege, and we will conclude with some evidence of victims who fortuitously escaped death. During the course of the evidence we will also provide audio-visual material showing maps of the area and actual video footage taken at the time of the events alleged in the indictment. As mentioned earlier, the charges are Grave Breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Violations of the Laws of Customs of War, and Crimes Against Humanity. Counts 1, 2 and 3 are concerned with the beatings that took place in the farm building at Ovcara and counts 4, 5 and 6 are concerned with murders that took place at the mass grave site. None of the counts are in the alternative, and the elements of the offence are as follows: Grave Breaches. The common element is that the victims are persons protected by one of the Geneva Conventions. The jurisdictional prerequisite is that the actions or omissions occurred during an armed conflict or partial or total occupation, in which the law for international armed conflict applies. Article 2(c) providing for wilfully causing great suffering. The elements of that offence are that the accused (or a subordinate) committed a specified act or omission upon the victim, and that the accused (or a subordinate) committed the act or omission with the intention of unlawfully inflict great suffering, and that suffering was thereby inflicted. Article 2(a) deals with wilful killing. The elements of that offence are that the victim is dead, and the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission in which the accused (or a subordinate) participated, and that at the time of the act or omission the accused (or a subordinate) had the intent to kill or inflict grievous bodily harm upon the victim. In relation to Violations of the Laws or Customs of War (counts 2 and 5) Article 3 of the Statute provides that the Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons violating the laws or customs of war and specifically states that the enumerated offences in subparagraphs (a) to (e) are not exhaustive. In addition to other codifications of the laws and customs of war, Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and the 1977 Additional Protocols I and II of 1949 are included within the parameters of our Statute. Further, there are recognised minimum rules applicable to all armed conflicts regardless of their classification which the enumerated offences in Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions apply. The common element of these offences are that the act or omission occurred during an armed conflict, either international or internal or both. Common Article 3 dealing with Cruel Treatment; the elements of that offence are that the accused (or a subordinate) committed a specified act or omission against the victim, the victim was a non-combatant or hors de combat, and that the accused or subordinate thereby intended to subject the victim to cruel treatment. Murder, as covered by Common Article 3, the elements are that the victim is dead, that the victim was a non-cambatant or hors de combat, and that the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission in which the accused (or a subordinate) participated and at the time of the killing the accused (or a subordinate) had the intent to kill or inflict grievous bodily. Finally, Crimes against Humanity, counts 3 and 6. Crimes against Humanity are serious offences directed against persons as part of a widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population. The victims of crimes against humanity constitute a wider class than those who are covered by Articles 2 and 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal, and may include fellow citizens of the person committing offences as well as stateless persons. Although both are directed against a specific group, crimes against humanity can be distinguished from genocide in that they do not require an intent to destroy the group, only proof that the act was part of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population is required. The common element is that the act or omission was part of a widespread systematic attack against a civilian population. Dealing specifically with the offences charged in the indictment, namely, Article 5.1, Inhumane Acts. The elements of that are that the accused (or a subordinate) committed a specific act or omission against the victim, that the act or omission of the accused (or a subordinate) was unlawful and included but was not limited to one or other of the following: An outrage upon the person's dignity; a sentence without proper trial; other unlawful acts intended to impair the physical, intellectual or moral integrity of the victim. Dealing with murder, the elements are much the same as those already specified for this offence, namely, that the victim is dead, that the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission of the accused (or a subordinate) and at the time of the killing the accused (or a subordinate) had the intent to kill or inflict grievous bodily harm on the victim. Briefly now turning to the provisions of Rule 61: The decision that has to be made under Rule 61 is that if the Trial Chamber is satisfied on the evidence that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed all or any of the crimes charged in the indictment it shall so determine. This to be contrasted with what happens when an indictment is confirmed under Article 18(4) of the Statute, for in that case it is for The Prosecutor to decide that a prima facie case exists before he embarks upon preparing an indictment. Once the indictment is prepared by The Prosecutor, it is submitted to the confirming judge to satisfy him or herself that the decision by The Prosecutor that a prima facie case exists is appropriate. Thus, the confirming judge does not make a fresh determination on whether or not there is the prima facie case but, rather, tests the decision of The Prosecutor, in order to see that his decision is correct. As the primary determination prior to confirmation is by The Prosecutor, where reasonable minds could differ as to whether a prima facie case exists or not, emphasis, it is submitted, should be placed on the reasonableness or otherwise of The Prosecutor's determination. In dealing with the assessment of whether or not there are reasonable grounds for belief that the evidence should be viewed in the light most favourable to the Prosecutor, all available inferences, it is submitted, should be drawn in favour of the Prosecution and apparent inconsistencies are not called upon to be resolved. As to the meaning of prima facie case, Rule 47 of the Rules of the Tribunal used the phrase "reasonable grounds for believing that a suspect has committed a crime within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal". These words were considered by His Honour Judge Sidhwa on 29th August 1995 when confirming an indictment, case No. IT-9512-1. He summarised those terms in following words: "... the word reasonable is associated with what is fair, moderate, suitable, tolerable, that which is not immoderate or excessive. The expression "reasonable grounds" is used; not overly convincing, substantial or conclusive grounds. Reasonable grounds, therefore, point to such facts and circumstances as would justify a reasonable or ordinary prudent man to believe that a suspect has committed a crime". If your Honours please, there is no basis for drawing any distinction between the test to be applied by the confirming judge under Rule 47 and the test to be applied by this Chamber under Rule 61. Rule 61(C) uses the same terms as appears in Rule 47(A), namely, "reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed ... the crimes charged in the indictment". Those, your Honour, are the matters of law that I wish to address your attention to; unless there are any other matters that I may assist you with, that is my opening. I now call Dr. James Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you call the witness, Mr. Gow, I wanted just very briefly to come back to these charges. The indictment that was confirmed by Judge Riad bore on three counts, serious breaches of the Geneva Convention, violations of the Customs of War and Crimes against Humanity. This comes under both categories, that is to say, injuries and murder. My question is in the presentation you just made, counsel, do you consider that you have added to your indictment? The reason I am mentioning this is because you said there was no alternative, that everything was cumulative, as it were. So my understanding was, and I think it on behalf of all three of us, I thought there was an alternative as regards the possibility of the serious injury and the homicide or murder in the case of the fact that the victims have disappeared, so there is room for doubt; or I had understand that it was cumulative in so far as a person might have disappeared but before that then seriously injured and bodily harm inflicted to them. But I have the impression that you have added to your indictment, as it were. Can you confirm that for me or not, or is this just a matter of a different presentation, particularly, in connection with the alternative? We are not trying to go into anything theoretical here; we have to see to it that the rules are followed for all the parties involved. So we want things to be transparent and straightforward. This is why we would like to ask you what your feeling is on the presentation you have just made in respect of the counts so that we will see that subsequently in the transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEIMANN
utterances.text: May it please your Honours, we say that the counts are all cumulative. They are not expressed in the alternative. In fact, there are two specific events; the first being the beatings, the second being the killings. We seek to proceed with those charges as separate events. In addition to that, we say that there is all justification to distinguish them between Grave Breaches and Violations of the Laws and Customs of War. We do so on the classification of the persons affected by the crimes committed against them, namely, you may have a number of groups which I am not in a position or I do not wish to go into specifying at the moment, but you could have, for example, people who were combatants who were hors de combat, you may have people who were simply innocent stand-by civilians standing by who were ensnared in all this; you may also have persons who were not of the group, the Croatian group, not of the same group. It is possible that all of those three eventualities may be the case. We say that the width of the indictment is necessary for all of those reasons and that, therefore, they are cumulative.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just give you an example, counsel, if I may? For example, when it comes to grievous bodily harm -- I say this because the accused is not present so it is very important in terms of the rights of the Defence -- when you take grievous bodily harm category, bodily injury, I would just like to understand; somebody who is beaten up and he is beaten seriously but is not killed, do you see that as being cumulative to your mind that that be categorised as a Grave Breach to the Geneva Convention to see that it is to cause serious bodily harm, suffering? Is that cumulative with count 2, Violations of the Customs of War, where you refer to Article 3, Cruel Treatment, since beating someone is cruel treatment, so is it also cumulative with count 3 which is Crimes against Humanity, Inhumane Acts, Article 5(i), because beating someone may also be regarded as an inhumane act. The judges would like to have an explanation of this. So do you give the court the possibility of choosing or do you see this as being serious bodily harm, Grave Breach, Violation of Customs of War and an Inhumane Act? We would really like to hear your view on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, we do. We point to distinctions that exists between each of these types of offences. We say that that entitles us to charge the three of them cumulatively. What may be troubling your Honours is what to do with it at sentence, but that is another question. The court may say: "When it comes to sentence we are only going to deal with it as if it was one", but that is another matter entirely. We submit our indictment is based upon the fact that each of these particular types of charges encompass and envisage different circumstances and, as a consequence of that, there is two possibilities; one is that a particular individual may well fit within two of them, or three of them, and so in that event a victim to those crimes fitting within all three, we submit, it is appropriate that we charge. Alternatively, there may be different classifications of people within the overall group. So it is necessary to have the three there, so that if one clearly does not fall within one group, then they are covered by the other. In that event, it would be not in a sense cumulative, but one would fall away and would not apply. But it is possible, in our submission, and appropriate, to charge three events because there are circumstances where the three particular offences could apply to the one individual.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. Now I believe you wish to call Mr. Gow is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct. DR. ANDREW JAMES GOW, called Examined by Mr. Niemann

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gow, would you like to put the head set on? Can you hear me? Could you please stand up to make your declaration and to introduce yourself to the Tribunal, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Andrew James WilliamGow and I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You be can seated. Prosecuting counsel? MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, you are a Political Scientist with positions of lecturer in the Department of War Studies, Kings College, London, and a Research Associate for Defence Studies, University of London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Formally, you were a Research Officer for the Centre of Defence Studies and before that lecturer on Soviet and Eastern European Affairs at Hatfield Polytechnic in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you hold the degree in Doctor of Philosophy from the University of London where you prepared your doctoral thesis on Yugoslavia at the school of Slavonic and Eastern European studies? That is correct. For the past several years has your work been concentrated on the former Yugoslavia, particularly its military and political affairs, and have you written and lectured extensively about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your evidence based upon your personal knowledge and drawn from your own work and that of other recognised scholars in this field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you used published reports, military and civilian writing, speeches and other official documents from the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of relevant Yugoslav language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you based your research on conversations with knowledgeable persons and witnesses' statements and documents made available to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since 1988 have you published numerous books and articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you given evidence before this Chamber of the Tribunal on a previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, in the case of the indictment against Dragan Nikolic for cases in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, concerning the former Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia prior to 1991, can you tell the court about the political composition of that Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federation comprised six republics, Slovenia, Croatia Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Macedonia and Montenegro and within Serbia there were two autonomous provinces; in the north the province of Vojvodina, and in the south the province of Kosovo. The six republics were taken to be the federating elements, but the two autonomous provinces within Serbia also played a role at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look now, please, at the map? If your Honour pleases, I would ask the assistance of Miss Sutherland in order to present this material on the machine. Dr. Gow, I would like you, please, if you would, to look at this document which we have styled The Prosecutor's Exhibit 1. Your Honours, I think you need to press the button "video monitor" in order to receive the image of this document when Dr. Gow refers to it in the course of his evidence. Dr. Gow, would you please look at the map that is now shown to you as Prosecutor's document 1, Exhibit 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, firstly, what is this map a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a map of the -- showing the territories of the republics and autonomous provinces which constituted the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia before its dissolution in 1991, and indicates -- the republics and provinces I identified also identifies the capitals of each of the republics and provinces and, because of the relevance to the present case, the town of Vukovar is also marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might just point to that town of Vukovar now? This map was prepared under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just by reference to that town, could you please point out the various political entities that went to make up former Yugoslavia prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The six republics, as I said, were Slovenia, which is in the north, Croatia, forming the bow shape around the north and the western part of the country, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the central republic, Montenegro in the southwest, the smallest, in the south Macedonia and the largest of them was Serbia with the two provinces, Kosovo in the south and Vojvodina in the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that, Prosecution document No. 1. I tender that document. Dr. Gow, can you tell the Chamber of the ethnic composition of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic Federation. The population comprised overall around 34, 35 per cent Serbs, who were the single largest group, and also comprised ethnic groups, Croats, Slav Muslims in Bosnia and in parts of Serbia it included Slovenes and Macedonians who were Slavonic peoples but distinct groups, and it also included non-Slavonic populations, small numbers of Hungarians and Slovaks, other central East European peoples, and the Albanians who were a non-Slavonic people as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that is now shown to you, Prosecution Exhibit 2? Firstly, can you tell me what this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map showing the distribution, the ethnic distribution, of the single largest group in any particular area on the territories of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. It shows that in each of the republics, I would point out that it shows the single largest group which does not necessarily mean an absolute majority. Many parts of the country were very mixed, so it may only be a relative majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This map prepared under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was prepared under my supervision by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour. It is Prosecution Exhibit 2. Would you look at the next document, please Dr. Gow, that I show you? Firstly, can you tell us what that document represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a table indicating the proportions of each of the ethnic groups within the total population of the SFRY, Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, according to the censuses taken in 1981 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that prepared under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was prepared at my direction by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour, marked as the Prosecution Exhibit 3. Dr. Gow, was there any ethnic group wholly contained within any one republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to say that no ethnic group was wholly contained within any one of the republics within the SFRY. Slovenia was the most ethnically homogeneous of the republics with around 90 per cent of the population being ethnic Slovene? In the republic of Serbia, for example, around two-thirds of the population were Serbian, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina it was a very mixed population, around 44 per cent Muslims, 30 or so per cent Serbs and 17 per cent Croats. In Croatia, again the proportions were around three-quarters Croats to a quarter non-Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now, please, look at the next document that is shown to you, Prosecution Exhibit 4? By looking at that document, are you able to tell me what it represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It represents the percentage that the single largest group in each of the Republics constituted under the 1981 census in the period running up to the dissolution of the SFRY. You can see, as I said, 90.5 per cent of the population of Slovenia comprised ethnic Slovenes; in Croatia it was 75.1 per cent out of a total population of around 4.6 million, and in Serbia around two-thirds of the population of the republic as a whole; although you will note that within narrow Serbia, without the provinces, that rises to 85 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, was this document prepared under your supervision and direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was prepared under my supervision in the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that as Prosecution Exhibit No. 4. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, were there any variations in the religious beliefs of various ethnic groups in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federative Republic embraced a number of different religious groups. The major groups were Roman Catholics, mostly in the western part of the country, Slovenes and Croats; the second -- another large group was the orthodox church. There were a separate Serbian, Montenegrin and Macedonian orthodox churches, although the Serbian orthodox church was the oldest of these and, perhaps, the major one. There was Islam as a religion which was embraced by the Muslims, the Slav Muslims, in Bosnia and in Serbia as well as by the majority of the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the historical and political background of former Yugoslavia, when was the entity known as "Yugoslavia" first proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was first proclaimed on 1st December 1918. It was proclaimed as the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. It changes its name to the kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now ask you to look at documents, Prosecution Exhibits 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, a cumulative set of maps which I shall ask you to deal with together. Perhaps dealing with them in number order; dealing firstly with No. 5, can you tell us what that represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map represents the territories which went to make up Yugoslavia prior to the Balkan wars in the period 1911, 1913. It shows the territory. The colours are not distinct on the image I have on the monitor, but it shows the territory which was independent Serbia, which had become independent in the course of the 19th century, and in a slightly different shade of red which is not, as I say, distinct on this map, but it runs approximately along the line -- the line there that I just indicated, the territories acquired by Serbia in the course of the Balkan Wars of 1911/13, and also indicates with the pink colour area acquired by Montenegro which had been independent as well throughout the period, most of the period, of Ottoman occupation of the peninsular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next map, Prosecution Exhibit No. 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map shows the territories which went to make up Yugoslavia in 1918 when it was first proclaimed, the territories now encompassing the whole of what was independent Serbia; the territory of Montenegro, which I shall indicate there, and territories which had previously been until 1918 were part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire; Bosnia and Herzegovina which was a principality; the joint realm of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia, which more or less comprises the present Republic of Croatia but not exactly; the Banat region, most of which is now present day Vojvodina in the north, and the territories which went to constitute Slovenia at this stage were not all forming part of Yugoslavia, although, I think, if I may point out, in drawing up the map there has been an error on the line here, but parts of it were with Italy here in the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. The next document, document 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map shows the administrative structure of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia following the Royal Declaration of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and Royal Dictatorship in 1929. The then king, King Alexander, made an effort to take away some of the importance of historical territories and identities to try to forge a Yugoslav identity by restructuring the country administratively this shows the territories, the administrative districts, which were part of that arrangement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document shows the boundaries of the Croatian Banovina within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The Croatian Banovina was established in 1939 by an agreement between Croat politicians and the Royal Government. The first Yugoslavia had been plagued by many disputes and many difficulties, particularly of an ethnno-national character. It was felt one of the solutions to that problem would be to give an area which would be under large -- the autonomous Croatian rule within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The coast line and the red area on the map marks the boundaries of that Banovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think on the map there is shown the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vukovar town is shown on that map and indicated there, and being just inside the Banovina border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to point in part to the course of the Danube river that is shown on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Danube river approximately follows this part of boundary and runs on through the other part of the boundary to Belgrade. That is an approximation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The next document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map shows the territorial disposition during the Second World War. The white area shows the territory of the independent state of Croatia. It was ruled by a group called the Ustasha who were backed by the Axis powers and had been installed in power by the Axis powers following the German invasion of April 1941. It shows areas, also the areas of influence of Italy towards the Dalmatian coast and of Germany within the central lands within that independent state of Croatia. It also shows territories which were ceded to Italy, encompassing Istria and parts of Slovenia and to Germany encompassing other parts of Slovenia, and territories which came under other control, Italy in the south, Montenegro and parts of Kosovo; Bulgarians taking parts of Macedonian and southern Serbia, Serbia itself becoming a protectorate of the Germans under a local Serbian administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, would you look at the next -- that is all of those documents. I tender those, if your Honour pleases, as Prosecution marked exhibits 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9. Looking at the next map that you are shown, can you tell us what that indicates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map indicates the spread of orthodox populations on the territories of the former Yugoslavia prior to its formation in 1918. You will note that are two shades of green; the deeper shade of green indicates the areas in which there was an absolute majority for the orthodox, and the lighter shade of green indicates areas in which there was a mixed population, but a significantly large relative majority for the orthodox. The map indicates the entirety of orthodox populations. Therefore, it makes no distinction between Serbian orthodox and other branches of the orthodox church. So, for example, that Macedonian orthodox church which was not established until later is indicated as being Serbian orthodox for the purposes of this map. The importance of this is to understand that as Yugoslavia was formed it was formed from the territories which went to comprise, first, the Royal Yugoslavia and then the Socialist Federal Republic, but that Yugoslav state represented two ideas; one was the idea of a formation in which there could be self-determination for all the various peoples which I have mentioned in the course of giving evidence so far, but it was also a state in which all the Serbs would be able to live together. The spread of the population, of the orthodox population, on this map indicates the territories which would be included within a state which would enable all the Serbian orthodox populations to come together. A consequence of that, you see, is that there is a strong mixed population in parts of Croatia and in parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that map as Prosecution Exhibit 10. Dr. Gow, where did the concept of the unified Yugoslavia come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was just indicating, there was two ideas leading to the formation of a Yugoslav state: One was a state in which all the Yugoslav peoples, the south Slav peoples, Yugoslav, south Slav, would come to live together and have a framework for self-determination. This was on the basis of thinkers largely in the Habsburg Empire, predominantly Croat intellectuals, who saw that south Slav peoples had enough in common that they should be able to share a common life, and that many of them or most of them would be too weak on their own to have a State at that stage in history. The alternative idea which emerged as Serbia itself became independent from the Turkish Ottoman Empire during the course of the 19th Century was that a state should be created in which all the Serbs would live together. The previous map we saw indicated the spread of orthodox Serbian populations, and the previous maps showed that the area that was narrow Serbia and the territory acquired in the course of the Balkan Wars, that left many of the orthodox populations still outside the then Serbia in parts of Bosnia and in parts of Croatia. There was the aspiration that a state would be formed in which they would all come together. So the creation of Yugoslavia was both the framework for all the Serbs to live together and the frame-work for self-determination, in theory, of the other south Slav peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if any, impact did the First World War have on the formation of Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The First World War, the outcome of the First World War, was significant in that promises had been made by the allies to Italy under the Treaty of London in 1915, by which parts of the territory of what is now Slovenia and Croatia was promised to Italy as a reward for entering the war on the allies' side. Although there were two ideas about forming a Yugoslavia and there were lots of discussions in the course of the First World War, the particular Yugoslav state which was formed in 1918 was largely an expression of the existing Serbian Kingdom, because the threat of Italian annexation made the Habsburg south Slavs turn to Serbia for, in a sense, protection. So it would, therefore, form a state on the terms of the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if any, were the major political developments or events in Yugoslavia between the First and the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the State was formed in that way, as an extension of the Serbian Kingdom, many of the other peoples, particularly the Croats, were very unhappy about this. There was a lot of political discontent. The country was rife with problems, particularly nationalism. This led to the declaration of the Royal Dictatorship I mentioned in 1929 following the shooting of the leader of the Croatian Peasant Party, and later on led to the arrangement by which the Croatian Banovina, which we saw on one of the maps before, was created.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of the unified state of Yugoslavia at the eve of the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although some compromise had been reached in the establishment of the Croatian Banovina, it was still the case that the state was largely divided, was gripped by many political ethno-national problems and when the Axis powers invaded it was very easy for them to take over and to dismember the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the main features of the impact of the Second World War on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Second World War in ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could we have a break, perhaps, at 11.15 because we do not want to break at the wrong moment. It would make life easier for everyone, also for the interpreters. I was wondering whether you might have a natural break in the discussions, so that I said we might have a break at 11.15. 4 MR. NIEMANN: Certainly, your Honour. I will finish this question and it is convenient to break then. (To the witness): Perhaps you might finish the answer, if you have any more to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am happy to answer now or to answer after a break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, please answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Second World War in Yugoslavia was an extremely complex affair. There were three main groups. It was a combined war of national liberation, a combined -- a civil war and a revolution. The main groups involved were the Croatian Ustasha who were helped into power by invading Axis powers within the independent state of Croatia; a group called the Chetniks, Serbs loyal to the old Royal Yugoslavia who formed a resistance movement under the leadership of Colonel Draza Mihajlovic, and the Communist led partisan movement under leadership of Josip Broz Tito who was to become President of Yugoslavia after the war. The war, as I said, was very complex. There were many aspects of it which I would go into, but with the request for a break in mind, I would rather than beginning that now, I think it might be appropriate to end my answer for now here and to pick up again after a break, if we are going to have one, if that is agreeable to your Honours?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that is a convenient time for your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. The session is suspended until 11.35. (Adjourned for a short time)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting counsel, you have the floor, and so does the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Gow, was ethnic persecution adopted by the participants as a feature of their campaign during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was. There were a number of incidents, of actions committed by all sides which could be considered to be atrocities; Serbian Chetniks, for example, massacring Muslims. However, the Ustasha independent state of Croatia in particular adopted a policy of ethnic purification, what perhaps today we would call "ethnic cleansing". It had a policy by which it intended by statements of senior officials to kill a third, expel a third and convert a third of the orthodox population within Croatia. Maybe if I might ask for the map of the Second World War, the division of territory in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could assist me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Exhibit 9 could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not have an image.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Press "video monitor".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will see that there were two areas of influence by the axis powers: the Italian zone and the Germany zone. The bulk of what might be called the ethnic persecution took place within the areas under the Germany zone and were carried out by the Ustasha in the border areas of Croatia, primarily in the border areas of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, where there were strong Serbian populations and mixed communities. The Ustasha programme played very significantly into the hands of the communist led partisans. The partisans were already strong in parts of southern Serbian and were strong in the areas under Italian occupation because the people in Dalmatia, both Serb and Croat, resented that their territory had been put under Italian population and, therefore, would support ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry, there is a translation problem. I did not hear the response of the expert. Excuse me Mr. Gow, would you mind starting again, I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am happy to start again. There were two zones of influence over the axis occupations in the areas of former Yugoslavia: one under the Italian zone and the other under the Germany zone. The ethnic purification programme carried out by the Ustasha regime occurred predominantly in the border areas of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the areas of Banja Luka, Banijal, Kordun and in north western Bosnia. That programme fed into the hands of the Communist led partisan movement. The partisans were strong in parts of southern Serbia and in parts of Dalmatia where the population resented being placed under Italian occupation and, therefore, supported the resistance and went to the partisans, although some of them went with Chetniks. In particular, the partisans fled from the campaign of attempted ethnic purification. Serbs, who were aware of massacres taking place, tended to side with the partisans because they were providing resistance to the Ustasha regime and also many Croats who formed part of the Anti-Fascist in Croatia joined in the partisan movement providing resistance both to the Ustasha regime and to the axis powers occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to look at the document which you are now shown numbered Prosecution Exhibit 11. Tell us, if you would please, Dr. Gow, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is a copy of an Article taken from the Journal Foreign Affairs, in the summer of 1993, and it contains evidence of a quotation which is significant in understanding the Second World War in Yugoslavia and the programme of ethnic purification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might show us an excerpt of that which is on what page of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The excerpt is on page 116.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just point directly to it. I will ask that it be magnified so we can read with greater clarity the relevant the section of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document includes a quotation from Mile Budak who is not named here but was the deputy leader of the Ustasha, the so-called Deputy Poglavnik and was Minister of Education. On 22nd June 1941 he was reported as having made the following comment in a speech you will see identified. The programme was: "One third of the Serbs we shall kill, another we shall deport and the last we shall force to embrace the Roman Catholic religion and thus meld them into Croats."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit, if your Honour pleases, as Exhibit 11. Dr. Gow, what were the policies adopted by Tito and his followers during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The partisan movement led by Josip Tito organised by communists aimed to gain support from all the different ethnic communities with a view to creating a new Yugoslavia. That new Yugoslav state would be one in which there was a place for the various communities. The partisans promoted the idea of brotherhood and unity; this was their slogan for mobilising support, and they were not the preserve exclusively of any single ethnic group within Yugoslavia, unlike the Ustasha or the Chetniks each of which was predominantly loyal to either a particular strand of Croatian opinion or a particular strand of Serbian opinion. The partisan movement offered the prospect of a new Yugoslavia which would be a federal Yugoslavia which by being federal would rectify many of the problems which had bedeviled the first Yugoslavia, that is the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. It would create a federal structure in which the various different national communities would each have something that would be their own so-called "nation state formation". This was based on the programme during the war of building government on liberated territory as they went. So the federal structure at one level emerged through the people's council established by the partisans in the course of the war. So alongside the military campaign to defeat the Ustasha, to defeat the Chetniks and to expel the axis powers, they were also in the process of building governments political on the territories under partisan control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you comment on the specific developments in Croatia during the period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was significant that the partisan movement in Croatia developed with a very strong Croatian identity. The Anti-Fascist of Croatia became very strong, particularly in the Dalmatian areas. For most of the war until very late stages the main parts of Croatia and Slavonia were still under Ustasha control. The partisan movement in Croatia was able to gain support on the one side from Serbs because they were obviously opposing the Ustasha programme, on the other from Croats and from others in Dalmatia in particular, because it seemed to offer the kind of solution to the problem for the Croats that they felt had not been present in the first Yugoslavia. It was, therefore, a very strong autonomous council within the federal partisan communist movement, one which at the end of the war Tito saw as being very strong and as a result of which he took measures by taking the leader of that movement, Andrija Hebrang, to Belgrade to try to take away some, diffuse some of the potency in the strength of that independent communist party led movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Second World War continue to have an influence on Yugoslavia throughout the postwar period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is fair to say that the Second World War in the post Second World War period. On one level this was because the legend of the partisan success was an important founding myth within the second Yugoslavia. The second Yugoslavia was very much a state which was based on the success of Tito and the partisans in the Second World War. It continued to be important as well because one thing that Tito and partisans did not do was to try to rectify, to account for many of the awful things which had happened in the Second World War. At one level many Croats felt that the Croatian population as a whole was being identified as being Ustasha, and because it was not possible openly to discuss these matters, there were many questions which were left unresolved, many figures for people killed in a particular place which were never properly addressed. Therefore, this was an issue which retained potency. In particular, in some of the areas I mentioned on the borders of Croatia and Bosnia, I think it is fair to say that the Serbian population continued to see itself as being in a vulnerable position, although it was significantly disproportionately represented within the official structures of the Republic of Croatia; something like about -- although 12 per cent of the population may estimate say, 60, per cent of the Police Force, for example, were taken from the Serbian communities. So on the one side the Serbs continued to feel vulnerable, but on the other the Croats tended to see the communist rule, the partisan movement, in a large sense as reflecting the interests of the Serbian group within Croatia. So at one level there continued to be tensions. There were specific examples of this, I think. Some of this resonance continued in areas such as Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with Vukovar, are you able to comment on whether the Second World War had an impact on that area and what its impact was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vukovar was one of the last areas to fall to the partisans. I think it was as late as April 13th 1945, although I am not certain about the date, but it was in the final campaign as the partisans moved through Slavonia on towards Zagreb. It was an area in which in the course of the war there had been a change in the balance of the populations. Serbs had been killed or expelled and predominantly Ustasha families were reported by the partisans to have been moved into that area. I think it is significant that that is a question which may have had resonance which continued through the post Second World War years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What constitutional measures were adopted by the communists after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The partisan movement put in place formally a federal structure of the six republics and two autonomous provinces that I mentioned before. At this stage the provinces were known as autonomous regions and did not have the real autonomy which later they were to gain in the 1970s, but they were always there formally. The federation itself was largely borrowed as a model from the Soviet Union and the communists did not intend for it to have any real meaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did Tito play in the federal system that was established in Yugoslavia following the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tito was the linchpin of the federal system which evolved. Tito as the leader of the wartime movement had enormous personal authority. In 1948 he was the figure who stood up to Stalin as Yugoslavia was expelled from the communist movement. He therefore had enormous personal authority. In a system which through its evolution gradually came to give more and more power decentralised into the republics, Tito was the figure which could bring everything together. He could knock heads when there were disputes. His role, therefore, was extremely important and it was after Tito died that many of the issues which in the past through personal authority he might have been able to resolve -- in the past he might have been able to resolve certain problems through his personal authority. Without Tito there it became increasingly difficult to find solutions to those problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the most significant political developments in Croatia in this post World War Two period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most significant developments in Croatia I think in the political sphere have to be seen to be the growth of a nationalist movement in the late 1960s leading to the so-called Croatian spring of 1971. This was a time in which a group of intellectuals began, first of all, to look at language issues and to complain about the way in which Serbo-Croat dictionaries were written, in which Serbian variants were taken to be the norm and Croatian variants either ignored or treated as dialects. This grew into a broader movement, moving from culture into the political sphere, looking for the assertion of a greater Croatian identity, looking at the proportion or the allegations about the proportions of Serbs to Croats within the Interior Ministry, within the Police Force, within various other structures, particularly the defence forces and the armed forces. In general, it was a political movement which had a strong Croatian identity, was inspired by intellectuals, but was also embraced by leaders within the communist party of Croatia and, to a large extent looked back perhaps to the position in which the Anti-Fascist Council of Croatia had found itself at the end of the war. That was a movement which also unofficially embraced elements who were calling for Croatia to become independent, to seek its own membership of the United Nations. Eventually it was a movement which Tito and some of the Yugoslav Army generals saw as being disruptive, a factor leading to the possible disintegration of Yugoslavia. So Tito carried out a purge to remove the leadership in Croatia at that time and to restore for a period greater communist control over the structures in Croatia. At the same time, of course, Tito also carried out similar purges in Slavonia and Serbia of nationalists and liberal reformers in both cases. However, the effect of the events in 1971 were really to be shown in the 1974 Constitution where de facto authority was transferred to the republics. So, in a sense, those in the Croatian movement lost many of the arguments themselves at the time, that the arrangements of the 1974 Constitution made concessions to many of the things for which they were arguing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was there going on a process of centralisation and decentralisation in competing forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second Yugoslavia, Tito's Yugoslavia, with its federal structure but its communist party at the heart of it, was always an intention between centralisation and decentralisation. The trend was always gradually towards greater decentralisation. The decentralisation, however, was consolidated under communist party control within the republics. So instead of having a single communist party controlling the whole Federation, a situation emerged in which six communist parties within the republics, each was controlling its own fiefdom. It was that situation which in many ways contributed to the constitutional political past that Yugoslavia reached in the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to 1990 and beyond, did the events in Kosovo have any influence over what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The events in Kosovo had a significant impact. Those events concerned a movement first among Albanian students, but then more broadly for increased rights of political power for the Albanians within Kosovo. If I might ask for I think the second map showing the ethnic distribution I could illustrate what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. If your Honours will look at the province of Kosovo there in southern Serbia, you will see the blue on this map represents predominantly Albanian populated areas. Most of the province by the 1980s was, the overwhelming majority in the province was Albanian. In the process of liberalisation from the late -- mid-1960s onwards and embraced under the 1974 constitution, the province of Kosovo was given a significant degree of autonomy, although it was not given the same status as the republics, and was not given the quality of sovereignty which inhered in the republics. As a result of the changes, there were ethnic tensions as Albanians came to have jobs which in the past they did not have; Serbs were beginning to move out and there was also an Albanian language-educated Albanian elite emerging as a result of creating a university in the capital, Pristina. The Albanian students, however, in a very poor province did not have jobs to go to; there were a serious of issues connected with this, and increasingly they sought to have Kosovo elevated from the status of autonomous province to republic. This, of course, was a significant challenge to the Republic of Serbia and to the Serbian population. On both sides of that question, obviously, there was an issue. Albanian protests in 1981 led to a clamp down by the Serbian security forces, by Federal security forces, including elements of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, and through the course of the 1980s there was a series of arguments leading to events in the late 1980s when, under the leadership of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, Serbia took measures to remove the effective autonomy of Kosovo, although formally the autonomy remained. These steps were seen in other republics, and particularly in Croatia, as being the kind of moves which would lead to a stronger centralisation to greater Serbian influence and control within the Federation and, therefore, fed the strength of opinion within a republic like Croatia that there should be greater autonomy, greater moves to protect the sovereignty of Croatia as a republic within the Federation, although the stronger element in this movement at the earlier stages was Slavonia. As the changes came and the communist regimes fell in central and Eastern Europe, then in Croatia a nationalist government under President Franjo Tudjman was elected, the party of the Croatian Democratic Community, Hrvatska Demokratska Zajedinca, and that party was perceived by many of the Serbs as being pro-independence, which it was, and by being proindependence as being a reflection of the Ustasha regime of the Second World War which, I think, in fairness, for whatever might be said about it, it was not, but it did give rise to a growth of Croatian nationalism, and to increasing problems within the Republic of Croatia between the Serbian communities and the Croat communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps the Exhibit might be handed back? What changes did the new Croatian authorities bring in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were two significant measures adopted by the new Croatian authorities in 1990 which were to be significant in alienating the Serbian communities.
