The first of these was a change in the constitution of the Republic of Croatia which had previously defined Croatia as the state of the Croatian and Serbian peoples and others. The change, I believe, was made to the State of the Croatian people and Serbs and others. This was taken by the Serbs to diminish the place of the Serbs within it and was again seen as being a possible, by implication, move towards an independent Croatia which would have the resonances of the independent state of Croatia in the Second World War in their eyes. The second measure taken was a reorganisation of certain administrative structures and particularly within the Interior Ministry where, I believe I already mentioned, there were arguments about the proportion of Serbs within the structures of the Interior Ministry in the Republic of Croatia and within the Police Force. So certain administrative measures were taken in a process which, for the Croatian democratic community government, could be said to be purging communists from the partisan era was also, in effect, purging Serbs. It is not clear whether the intent was really to purge Serbs or communists. It probably makes little difference because the effect was the same. This added again to Serbian fears that things were going to happen to them. These were fears which the Serbian authorities in Belgrade, in particular, were able to play on and begin to give assistance to local Serbian communities in making stands against the Croatian authorities. One particular factor in all of this is that the reorganisation of the Interior Ministry and the Police Forces disestablished the police headquarters at Knin which had been under the control of the local Serbian police chief, Mile Marti}, and moved it into an area under Croatian control. That was seen as a significant challenge as well and Mile Marti} was to be the leader of an opposition movement in the Knin/Krajina area, and later to become President of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Serbian population in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I think I have been indicating, the Serbian population in Croatia in this period was becoming in many cases fearful. There was a degree of social disintegration, ethnic disintegration in the communities in Croatia. Antagonisms were rising in many of the rural areas. It is not clear that the same could be said for the urban areas such as the major towns such as Split or Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the JNA respond to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, the Yugoslav People’s Army, responded in some cases, possibly not as a whole, but in some cases local units giving assistance to the Serbs in the Krajina area, allowing them access to weapons, as a result of which the Serbs in the Kninska/Krajina area were able to erect barricades and to create an effective "no go" area for the Croatian areas in parts of the Republic of Croatia. The JNA began from, I think, April, from Easter, 1991 to be deployed outside its barracks as well in what it termed a peacekeeping role, a role separating the different communities. This increasingly appears to have become a role of protecting the Serbs or giving assistance to the Serbs within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this impact upon the whole process of dissolution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The impact on the dissolution of Yugoslavia as a federation was significant. The effect of this was to weaken what fabric there was of a multi-ethnic community within a republic such as Croatia, to put pressures on Bosnia and Herzegovina and to feed ultimately the more significant political constitutional disputes at the federal level between the republican governments about the future of Yugoslavia, what kind of Yugoslavia there would be and, in particular, a salient issue in the Republic of Croatia, of course, was whether or not Croatia would assert its sovereignty within a federation or a confederation and by doing that would possibly become either largely or wholly independent leaving the Serbs as a minority group within the boundaries of the Republic of Croatia. The Serbs, of course, were arguing against this and were getting backing from the Serbian regime in Belgrade to oppose any movement of this kind. So, the impact of this situation was reinforcing the overall processes leading towards the dissolution of Yugoslavia, adding fuel and an extra strand of ethno-national tension to the issues which were being discussed at the federal level as constitutional political matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, when did the Federation of Yugoslavia cease to exist or cease to function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SFRY ceased to function, in my judgment, on 15th May 1991. At that time the system for appointing a leader of the collective presidency, the Presidential Council, of SFRY broke down. If I may explain? The SFRY, as a federation, had a collective body at its head, comprising a representative from each of the six republics and from each of the two autonomous provinces, so, therefore, eight members. This mechanism established under the 1974 constitution involved a process of rotation. It was a set order where from one year to the next the rotation would take place. In the period leading up to May 15th, 1991, the presidency of the presidency had been held by a Serbian representative, Borisav Jovic. On May 15th the presidency was due to rotate to the Serbian (sic) representative, Stipe Mesic. The Serbian grouping led by Jovic, now including Serbian control representatives from Kosovo, Vojvodina and Montenegro blocked the automatic rotation. It was the first time, I believe, that anybody had ever called for a vote to confirm the rotation and, as a result, deadlock emerged in Yugoslavia and there was a crisis and, as a result of that, I would judge the federation no longer functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any events in the spring of 1991 which exacerbated the situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While these events were taking place at the federal level and some of the tensions I mentioned were occurring at the local level, it was significant that from the summer of 1990 onwards there began to be violent incidents in the republic of Croatia. There were, I believe, something over 0 small detonations, bombing incidents, attacks against railway lines and the like. I mentioned the Yugoslav People’s Army allowing Serbs in the Krajina area to get weapons in addition to those they got from the local police station, from Mr. Marti}. In other areas, at Pakrac on 2nd March and at Plitvice Lakes at the beginning of April, there were shooting incidents between local Serbs and Croatian authorities. In the second of those the Yugoslav people's army was deployed ostensibly as a peacekeeping force. There was one particularly nasty incident in the village of Borovo Selo in Eastern Slavonia within the Vukovar district which involved, first of all, a series of tensions had been emerging in that area for the month before. It would be difficult to go into it in detail, but there were, essentially, groups on either side, Croatian and Serbian, who were carrying out attacks against each other; some were between political gangster and paramilitary groups, maybe dropping grenades through people's doors, activities of this kind, creating tension and destabilization in the area. On 2nd May, two Croatian policemen were abducted by Serbian paramilitary groups. The Croatian response was to send in, I think, a large number of policemen, maybe 150. As a result of that incident, the Croatian authorities felt that their policemen had been trapped, and they were ambushed and 12 of the Croatian policemen died as a result of the incident. The reports indicated that a number of them had been mutilated as well -- an obvious reference to some of the atrocities which had taken place during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Croatia do when the federation itself collapsed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatia, as the federation was breaking down, hurriedly held a referendum on independence on 19th May 1991. The vote in the referendum was overwhelmingly in favour of Croatia's independence, either fully or within some kind of overall Yugoslavia community confederation at that stage, and on 25th June 1991, along with Slavonia it declared its independence from the federation. Dr. Gow, I would like to move on to the role and character of the Yugoslav national army, the JNA, in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Firstly, under the constitution, what was the position of the armed forces of Yugoslavia at the commencement of the armed conflicts in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might first be allowed to express an opinion on the use of the term "Yugoslav national army"? I think it would be appropriate to say "Yugoslav People’s Army", although the same word "narodna" in Serbo-Croat could be taken with either sense. It has to be understood that this was a communist movement and that the word "narod" was used in the sense of the people as in the people's republics of the other central Eastern European countries or the People's Republic of China. The role of the JNA was to be the first of a two tier defence -- the first level of a two tier defence structure. It would provide the first line of defence, hold any invading force until the second tier of the territorial defence forces could be mobilised. The territorial defence forces were organised by a republican secretariat for defence within each of the republics and were there to support an overall defensive effort against any potential invader and to act as a deterrent so that an invader would not come. The JNA was subordinate to the federal authorities, to a federal secretariat for the defence and, in addition its role in defence, it had a significant political role under the 1974 constitution. It was charged with theduty to protect the constitutional order of the SFRY and, in addition, at the same time it was given particular roles within the political sphere of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the communist party movement in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the intended purpose of the two tiered system of armed forces in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of the two tiered system was to have a more advanced and more professional force which would be able to hold off an invasion for 48 hours, if necessary, to allow the larger force, which would be mobilized, perhaps, up to 800,000 people, which would then be able to carry out gorilla resistance to make it too difficult for any occupier, any invader, to maintain control of the country. This works in two ways: (1) if an invasion actually comes in practice, the system is there in theory to make it too difficult for an occupier to maintain control of the territory, and in this much of the thinking goes back to the campaign that was carried out by the partisans in the Second World War. But, of course, beyond that the main idea was to send a deterrent message that it really would be too difficult for anybody thinking of invading Yugoslavia to maintain control and, therefore, would not be worthwhile invading in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did Tito consider that the JNA could play in Yugoslavia following his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the main reason that the JNA was given the significant role it was in politics after 1974 was that Tito judged that after he died within this balanced federal structure of republics and provinces, in which there were obviously sometimes mutually exclusive interests, the JNA politically would be able to represent a Yugoslav voice, a pan Yugoslav voice. Its interest would be, as his had been, in federal issues rather than in the exclusive issues of one of the particular republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did forces of disintegration of the federation have any impact on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The processes of disintegration had a significant impact on the JNA to the extent that in its political role it became ever harder for it to maintain a position of promoting a pan Yugoslav option. It made a difference in terms of the composition of the JNA to the extent that as a multi-ethnic army comprising conscript cadre in proportion with the population throughout the country in the 18 to 24 age band, the problems, the tensions, within the country were being reflected within the army as well, certainly, within the conscript cadre, to some extent probably within the officer core.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, going on from that, were there any other changes in the organisation of the military forces of Yugoslavia as a consequence of the forces of disintegration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of 1988 there was a significant, what was to become a significant, change in the structure of the JNA. It was reorganised from the previous system of army districts into a new system of military districts. One significant feature with reference to the present hearing was that the boundary, that the area in which Vukovar falls, I believe, changed, previously being part of the 5th Military District -- sorry, previously under the Zagreb command, the command of the Zagreb army district, that area came to be under the control of the 1st Military District headquartered in Belgrade. This, I think, was to have significant implications when the war came. Perhaps if I could ask for the first map I could quickly illustrate this? If your Honours will look at the map, you will see I have indicated the border between Croatia and the Serbian -- and the autonomous province of Vojvodina within Serbia. Until just after Vukovar, which is also marked, that border is formed by the River Danube. It is my understanding that the boundary between the army districts was formed by the river. As a result of the changes, the 1st Military District boundary was extended beyond the Danube for what were explained as "operational reasons" and came to include the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To sum it up, in other words, the JNA which was initially for the Vukovar area under the control of Zagreb as its headquarters was shifted to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps that Exhibit might be handed back? Dr. Gow, what was the principle of ethnic cleaning and how did it work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because Yugoslavia was a complex state, a federal state, composed of the republics and of all the different ethno-national communities, something called an ethnic or national key system operated so that in key federal bodies proportionality between the peoples of Yugoslavia, the communities making up Yugoslavia, would be maintained. In the case of the JNA, this was intended to try to preserve a balance in proportion with the share of the population within the officer core. Because there were certain imbalances in the officer corps, as a whole, as a result of tradition and recruitment patterns, this could not operate in the officer corps, as a whole, but what applied at the most senior levels in the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the document I am now showing you, the Prosecutor's Exhibit 12? Firstly, can you tell us what the document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- it is a document showing two tables which reflect the national composition of the Yugoslav people's army in the spring of 1991. The figures in the first able at the top of the page show the percentage of each particular national grouping in the first column within the officer corp. of the JNA and in the second column within the population of the SFRY as a whole. So, therefore, you will see if you look at the first line that Montenegrins were disproportionately highly represented in the officer corps being 6.2 per cent of the officer corps, but only 2.6 per cent of the total population of the SFRY. Similarly, you will see that whereas Slovenes comprise 7.8 per cent of the SFRY population at the time, they only make up 2.8 per cent of the officer corps; that the Serbs making up 36 per cent approximately of the total SFRY population comprised 60 per cent of the JNA officer corps as a whole. So, you will see these are the kinds of difficulties as a result of tradition, Serbs traditionally were expected to be more likely to go into the army, Slovenes, on the other hand, were in a more what might be regarded as a more advanced economic situation and tended to go for jobs in other spheres. This led to the imbalance in the officer corps, as a whole, giving it predominantly Serbian composition. The second table at the bottom gives the actual numbers for each group of the population at each of three relatively senior ranks within the JNA at the same time. The ranks of General, Colonel and Lieutenant Colonel. You will see again the same kind of disproportionate balance is reflected in the table there. You will see that there was only one Albanian, only one Albanian General but 77 Serbs. The Generals tending to be more reflective of the ethnic key principle and, as you move down, you see increasingly large number of Serbs at the level of Colonel and Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does this document come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was prepared at my instruction in the Office of The Prosecutor based on information provided by Defence publication in the SFRY sourced at the bottom to Ravija Obramba, a Slovenian periodical, in April 1991. A further set of figures, slightly different figures, were then issued and published in a newspaper, Politika, but not full figures about a month later reflecting broadly the same situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour. What impact did the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the armed conflict in 1991/92 have on the ethnic composition of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the JNA was radically altered by the course of armed conflict from being an army in which the officer corp. was predominantly Serbian, but which was clearly multi-ethnic and in which the conscript element was wholly multi-ethnic in proportion with the shares of the population as a whole. The vast majority of the non-Serbs left the service of the JNA, both at the officer corp. level and in the conscript cadre in the course of the armed conflict in Croatia, so that by the spring of 1992, it was estimated, I think, that out of a total of over -- whereas previously there had been 180,000 in the JNA, proportionately in the conscript cadre, proportionately spread between the different national communities, by the spring of 1992, I think, something like 11 per cent of the army as a whole, including the officer corp., were non-Serbs, and that figure includes the Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the document I now show you, Prosecutor's Exhibit 13? I think this document relates to that which you have just been speaking, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a graphic representation which illustrates what I was saying. You will see that the white column indicates the number of Serbs within the army as a whole putting that figure in June 1991 at a little under 40 per cent. That figure rises to 90 per cent by March 1992. It is showing the impact on the JNA turning it de facto from being an army in which people from all the Yugoslav communities are represented into an army in which predominantly the Serbs are represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification sake, the black -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The black column represents non-Serbs within the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the white is the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Represents the Serbs within the army, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first group relates to pre-1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, and the second column relates to March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is a very significant and dramatic change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It illustrates the significant impact that the armed conflict had on the composition of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 13. Did the JNA become Serbian as opposed to pro-Yugoslavian by a process of natural evolution or were there pressures brought to bear on the JNA in order to achieve this end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA could be said, clearly, to becoming de facto pro-Serbianian as a result of the changes in the composition of the army. There were also pressures brought to bear from political sources increasingly to make the JNA pursue something, to act in a Serbian interest. I think it is fair to say that, although the JNA leadership and the Serbian political leadership were not one, increasingly as the conflict developed their positions became very closely aligned and they were acting with the same objectives -- broadly with the same objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a consequence of the refocusing of the JNA, did it, in essence, become a Serbian military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is fair to say that to a large extent the JNA became de facto a Serbian force, although many, for some time many in the JNA leadership resisted, tried to resist the process of becoming completely a Serbian force, but the situation, I think, largely made it inevitably that eventually it would become a force which was, although called Yugoslav, essentially, acting in the interests of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What connection was there between the paramilitaries and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war in the -- the Yugoslav war of dissolution has been characterised by the presence of a number of paramilitary groups of different kinds, and in the war in Croatia, also the war in Bosnia, the paramilitary groups acted in some senses independently, but very often in co-ordinated action with the JNA acting as adjuncts of the JNA, adding greater manpower potential to the JNA which, as a result of the desertions that were reflected in the graph we saw before and in, as I was saying, the non-Serbs leaving the army, left the JNA short of manpower and increasingly relying on the paramilitaries in some situations to be foot soldiers, to be infantry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other reason why the JNA accepted the involvement of these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the essential reason that the JNA accepted the involvement of the paramilitaries was that there was a war that was taking place, they were increasingly, if not absolutely in the beginning, being placed on one side of that war. They were carrying out activities pursuant to the interests of a Serbian cause increasingly, but they were lacking the manpower to do that. In addition, I would say that it was significant that because of the Yugoslav identity and because many in the senior JNA leadership were still trying to hold back from being completely Serbianised, many Serbian nationalists saw the JNA as a Yugoslav force and, therefore, as a non-Serbian force. So, many of the paramilitaries would go to fight for a group labelled "Serbian" where they would not go and fight for the JNA and would not see the JNA as being a reliable fighting force in the cause of whatever Serbian interest it was they were pursuing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that there was a lack of confidence in the loyalty of the Serbs in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure entirely what you mean by that question, but if you mean were elements of the Serbian population lacking confidence in the JNA as a pro-Serbian institution, then I think that is the case, and that was one of the factors that I think I was just leading towards indicating why the paramilitary groups emerged in a situation of transition. They were able to attract a certain degree of support from nationalist Serbs who would not trust the JNA to act in their interests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did the paramilitary units play in Croatia and, more specifically, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A number of paramilitary groups were present in the Vukovar region. The paramilitary groups, these included the Tigers led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, known by the nom de guerre "Arkan", Chetnik forces and forces of the so-called Beli Orli White Eagles, loyal in the one case to Vojislav Seselj, and in the other to Dragoslav Bokan, according to reports. These forces were there, in part they involved criminal elements, but in part they were acting as the infantry and the foot soldiers for a JNA which was short of soldiers who were capable of going into built up areas and being prepared to do some of the things which the paramilitaries did carry out. It is a situation in which the paramilitary presence added to the destabalization I mentioned to the incidents in May in Borovo Selo where paramilitary groups were already present as part of the events which were destabilizing the situation in the Vukovar region. That destabilisation continued, and I think it is fair to say that the tension between the paramilitary groups on either side led to a particular situation in the Vukovar region where some of the things which happened were, perhaps, more intense than in other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the JNA to the declaration of independence by Croatia that you mentioned earlier in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA rejected the declaration of independence of Croatia and of Slavonia. It was deployed under an instruction from the federal government in Slovenia, but at the same time also began activities in Croatia. In effect, its role was within the framework of what was officially called separating the parties, but which I would say increasingly became one of supporting the Serbian effort to establish control of territories in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that particularly how it conducted the war against Yugoslavia in the second half of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the JNA conduct the war against Croatia in the second half of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA conducted the war in two, well, in fact, in three phases. In the first phase, I think there was a degree of uncertainty about what was going to happen, but the two-phased campaign began in July 1991 where preparations were made for a series of actions. That period ran through, I think, according to the Generals, until September, during which period preparations were completed. From the second half of August, I have dated approximately 19th August, the JNA began a campaign, whilst still officially acting within the rubric of separating the populations, to begin to establish the borders of the new entities, the borders of what they would regard as a mini Yugoslavia. The second phase, once these areas with predominantly Serbian populations had been controlled and areas, not all with predominantly Serbian populations, but most of them with predominantly Serbian populations, once these areas had been controlled and the Serbian population within the army's terms had been protected, there would then be the springboard for the second phase which would be attacks launched throughout the whole of Croatia to topple the Croatian authorities in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might add, that the second phase of this, I think it is fair to say, was abandoned in the face of the realities of the situation in which the JNA found itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at the document I now you show, Prosecutor's Exhibit 14? Firstly, what does this map represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a map which represents, which first shows the territorial division between the republics of the SFRY and the emerging states, but which also shows marked in green areas which were under Serbian control in the latter part of 1991, and in most of which there was at least one point where there was a significant -- the significant Serbian population. It also shows with the red arrows -- for example, I indicate the one there running from Mostar to Split on the coast -- the main axes of movement by the JNA, according to the record indicated by the head of the JNA at the time, the Secretary for Defence, General Veljko Kadijevic. The aim was to, these four main lines, axes of action which would cut Croatia and would be there for the framework for establishing territorial control within the boundaries embraced by those lines. In addition to this, the JNA was carrying out actions in Eastern Slavonia -- the area I have just indicated, the area near Vukovar -- but these activities, whereas the other activities were coming out of bases in Croatia and in Bosnia, these activities were being consolidated by forces from the 1st Military District in Belgrade. Whereas the other areas indicated in green had a predominantly Serbian population, only in one small part of this territory was there a majority Serbian population, but the JNA took control of large parts of this territory, including the agriculturally rich land of Baranja on the border with Hungary and with areas embracing some oilfields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The green areas represent the various theatres of operation of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA had three separate campaigns in the war in Croatia. It would regard Croatia as a whole as one theatre, I guess. The three separate campaigns that were being conducted were in the south in the Konavli strip down the coast leading to the Prevlaka peninsular. In this area, activity was almost entirely conducted by the JNA using Montenegrin -- using units from Montenegro, including Montenegrin reservists. That was purely JNA operation -- almost purely. The second area, the green marked on the map there, around the edges of north western Bosnia, including the Dalmatian hinterland, involved activity by the JNA and by local Serbian forces, largely Serbian forces, derived from using the structures of the old territorial defence system and acting in conjunction with the JNA, but local Serbs. Finally, in the third campaign area, distinct again, the JNA with largely JNA operations supported by aramilitary forces who were not predominantly local forces, but were coming across the border from the Republic of Serbia, and one of the most significant groups I have already mentioned, the Tigers of Zeljko Raznjatovic (Arkan), had their training camp at Erdut just inside the border with Croatia, just about there. So each of the campaigns had a different character; one was entirely JNA, one was JNA and local and the other was JNA and paramilitaries largely coming from Serbia. They were becoming involved in a series of clashes from the period before the declarations of independence, but in a significant way after the declarations of independence in conjunction with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was, just for a point of reference, the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was -- the first activity by Serbian groups was in the Knin area in August 1990. The other small local activity was in the areas here at Pakrac and Plitvice, somewhere there, in March/April 1991, and the incident at Borovo Selo was in May 1991 across there. But after the declarations -- and in the case of Knin the army gave weapons, or was reported to have given weapons to the local Serbs; in the case of Pakrac people said the army actually deployed out of its barracks -- but it was only after the declaration of independence that the JNA deployed out of its barracks in a significant way and only, I think, after mid-August 1991 that it began properly its campaign to establish control over the territories in conjunction with the various other groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any political action taken parallel with the military operation of the JNA in the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Political -- and indeed prior to the military action by the JNA. I was indicating that there had been some use of violence by Serbian communities versus the Croatian communities prior to the declarations of independence. On 21st December 1990 in the Knin area, the Serbian 'Autonomous Region of Krajina' was declared by the local Serbian authorities. That was followed, I think, on 26th February 1991 while the process of disintegration was taking place by the declaration of the Autonomous Region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem, which I have indicated there, the area in which Vukovar falls. On 19th December 1991, after approximately six months of fighting in Croatia, these two areas which under Serbian political, as well as military control, were consolidated with the declaration of the Republika Srpska Krajina establishing these areas as a separate political entity, and saying that this entity formed a part of Yugoslavia, that is, the Yugoslavia connected with Serbia and Montenegro. But, Serbia and Montenegro, as far as I am aware, at no stage indicated that they accepted that these areas joined them, so the areas then pursued the cause of independence from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender that Exhibit, your Honour. Dr. Gow, going back in more detail in relation to the Vukovar area itself, what was the status of the borders between the Vukovar area and the Vojvodina area following the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The border between Croatia and Vojvodina was established as the border between both Croatia and the Republic of Serbia, but also Croatia and the people's republic, the people's autonomous region of Vojvodina which was within Serbia. The border at the end of the Second World War was disputed between the anti-fascist Council and the communist party of Croatia, on the one side, which I indicated earlier had a strong independent character and, on the other, between the local district committee of the communist party of Srijem in Serbia and between the people's autonomous province of Vojvodina. The nature of the dispute concerned the division of the previous county of Vukovar which had extended into the area which was becoming the people's autonomous region of Vojvodina. Perhaps if I might ask for the map of the Croatian Banovina back? In fact, if I could ask for the Croatian Banovina map as well as the first map of the republics of Yugoslavia, it will help me to illustrate while I am dealing with the differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. 8 and No. 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (Handed) Thank you for your patience. You see Vukovar is there. The Vukovar county had been part of this area of the Croatian Banovina extending into almost to the very gates of Belgrade. If I can have the second map, you will see this is where the border was formed between Croatia and the people's autonomous region of Vojvodina. Therefore, part of the area which had been extending down to Belgrade, not all of which was Vukovar county, was being separated. So there was a dispute over where the border line should go. The dispute was put to a commission headed by a commission of the Anti-fascist Council of National Liberation of Yugoslavia headed by Tito's deputy, Milovan Dilas, and the committee adjudicated that the border should be formed by the River Danube, and that although there was a small Serbian majority in the northern district of Vukovar which would lie on the Croatian side of the boundary, it would remain as an isolated -- for a variety of geographic, economic reasons, it would lie on the western side, the western northern side of the Danube, and the Danube would form the border as far down as Ba~ko Novo Selo. This, of course, was an area of great dispute. I believe, if I recall, I mentioned that Vukovar had been one of the places, the last among the places under Ustasha control. It was also an area in which there had been significant ethnic changes. In the course of the war, the communist party of Srijem had put a submission to the Commission indicating that whereas, perhaps, something in the region of 2,000 Serbs had been killed or expelled either in Vukovar town or the villages around it, the Ustasha had also brought in approximately 2,000 people who remained there and continued to be Ustasha families. The area and other parts of this border were settled by the Commission but continued to be disputed. It is significant that one of the first major acts of ethnic cleansing also took place in this area at a town of Ilok just down the road, or what we term ethnic cleansing, when the JNA rounded up -- Ilok had a predominantly Croatian population or significant Croatian population, but was within Vojvodina on the other side of the border -- the JNA, I think, in September 1991 rounded up the local Croatian community and gave it instructions to leave and, with the assistance of international monitors, that population was moved from Vojvodina into Croatia. I think I am indicating that the area was controversial at the end of the Second World war and that, possibly, some of that controversy lingered into the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to the actual events of 1991, when did the JNA become involved in the Serbian side in the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be -- I do not think I would be able with complete assurance to say when the JNA became involved on the Serbian side in the Vukovar area or any other as a whole and absolutely, but it is clear that from the period after 19th August where I indicate that through observation of events, I think the second phase of the JNA -- sorry, the first phase of the JNA operations to create the new borders went into effect, that the JNA was working with the Serbian forces in the area and that the siege of Vukovar began somewhere around 24th -- in the days after 19th August, somewhere around 24th August, and was to last for 90 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Serbian forces were utilized in the attack against Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Vukovar area the Serbs used, made use of some of the paramilitary groups and, in addition to that, there were combined operations by units from the JNA combining naval, air and land forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what was the size of the JNA forces deployed in relation to the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There have been a variety of estimates that I have seen; some go as high as 50,000, those others put the figure around 30,000. I do not believe that anybody other than those in the JNA with the records would have an accurate account of that, but it is reasonable to say in excess of 30,000 were present at the siege of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what majority of these troops contributed, from what source were they contributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the troops involved at Vukovar came from the 1st Military District at Belgrade. They included predominantly units from 12 corps based at Novi Sad, also units from 24 corps at Kragujvac. They also included elite guards units and the mechanized elements from the mechanized division at Belgrade. They were supplemented by troops from the 5 corps at Tuzla and from the 2 corps based in Montenegro from the 3rd Military District.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of weaponry were used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA used a full range of weaponry in the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The siege of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, so used to say saying certain things -- in the siege of Vukovar, a full range including, I think, predominantly heavy mortars, 112 millimetre calibrated, 80 millimetre calibre; also significant numbers of heavy artillery ranging from 105 to 155 millimetre calibre. They were equipped with a significant number of tanks, significant enough for the Croatians, with what credibility, I do not know, to claim that they destroyed 200 tanks at Vukovar; the tanks being either old T34 tanks, middle-aged T55 tanks or quite a number of M84 Yugoslav production tanks of the latest generation. In addition, naval forces were used from the River Danube firing on the town and there was substantial use of the air force in some periods using ground attack aircraft to bomb the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the size of the Croatian forces in terms of numbers of troops against the attacking Serbian forces in approximate terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it is hard to establish precise figures. Some estimates, the highest estimates that I have seen, put the local Croatian defence force as high as 5,000. Most estimates put it in the region of 1500 to 1800 members, and 1800 is the figure cited by the leader of the primary defence organisation, a man called Milke Dedakovic, but the situation is unclear because I think there were three separate groups fighting within Vukovar on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the state of these Croatian forces at the commencement of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the commencement of hostilities the Croatian forces were mostly ill-prepared. I indicated there were three, I think there were three separate groups. One was a paramilitary group, the Croatian Council of Defence; the second was linked with the local Police Force and was part of the Croatian National Guards, Zbor narodne garde, and the main element came to be the Defence forces organised by Dedakovic that I mentioned. None of these forces was well equipped to fight a war at the beginning. The forces developed as the war went on and in terms of weaponry they were significantly out-gunned by the surrounding JNA Serbian forces. Estimates indicate that they may have had a few heavy artillery pieces, perhaps four or five, and that they were able to capture a small number of tanks as well. But, for the most part, they relied on using man portable anti-tank weaponry, which was brought in in small quantities either by parachute drops by Croatian military special forces or through the small route through the corn fields which was used to get access from the main part of Croatia to Vukovar in the period of the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. I have about another five or six questions to go, but I am very happy to do that after lunch if that is what your Honours would prefer or I am very happy to proceed now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting counsel, the members of the Tribunal and the President would like to ask a few questions. I would like to ask the witness a few questions and because your yourself have six more questions, I suggest, as we already agreed, that we adjourn the session and that we reconvene at 2.30. (Luncheon Adjournment)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, earlier in the course of your evidence just before the luncheon recess, you were speaking about the area known as Ilok. Would you like to add something further to your evidence in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to add as a point of clarification on that that when I was talking about the area being in dispute, I was making specific reference to the adjudication of the Committee of Anti-Fascist National Liberation Council of Yugoslavia in 1945/1946 about the delineation of the border between the People's Republic of Croatia and the people's autonomous province of Vojvodina, and it was their adjudication that Ilok should be within -- that the Ilok district should be within the province of Vojvodina. I should also make clear that the town of Ilok is presently within the Republic of Croatia. If I might add a further point of correction, I believe that I mistakenly indicated, having indicated that Borisav Jovic was the Serbian representative to the collective presidency of the SFRY, then went on to say that there was another Serbian representative, Stipe Mesic. Mr. Mesic was, in fact, the Croatian representative which, I believe you would agree, is a significant distinction to make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, Dr. Gow, we were talking just immediately before the break about the Croatian forces defending Vukovar, their composition and so on and their size. I would like you to tell us if you can from where the Croatian forces were derived primarily. I think that you have already touched on this in a previous answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I was beginning to say before the recess that my understanding is that there were three principal Croatian groups within the town, all very small. One was a paramilitary group known by the acronym HOS, the Croatian defence league; the second was organised by the local police Interior Ministry and was in a unit of the ZNG, Zbor nardne garde, the Croatian National Guard, and the final element which was perhaps the most significant was the defence forces organised locally by a man called Mile Dedakovic. I would add -- I think I said before but to be clear -- these forces comprise something in the region of 1800 personnel, for the most part lightly armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned lightly armed. Are you able to elaborate on the armaments that were available to the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian forces, I believe, had a small number of heavy artillery pieces available to them, maybe four or five what we would could call big guns, and a few tanks which they captured from the JNA forces, but primarily they relied on either light arms or on man portable anti-armour weaponry. I think I mentioned before the recess that they were able to get small supplies of these in either through the corn fields or by special forces groups parachuting in with them. But this was a very -- the amounts which could be brought in relative to the forces surrounding Vukovar were very small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on that, what was the ratio between the capability of the Serbs vis-a-vis their Croatian opponents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There have been estimates that between the 1800 or so, maybe up to a maximum of 5,000, which I think is unlikely, Croatian forces in the town and the surrounding 30,000 plus Serbian and JNA combined forces, the ratio is somewhere in the region of 1: in terms of personnel with, essentially, a small, brigade size force organised within Vukovar on the Croatian side and two operational groups organised outside the town encircling it on the Serbian JNA side; the northern one commanded by General Biorcevi} and the southern one commanded by Colonel Mile Mrk{i}. I think that ratio is estimated to be somewhere in the region of 1:15. In terms of the weaponry the difference was enormous; differences could run to 1:100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, did the JNA ultimately achieve its objective in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA and its Serbian allies in this context, I think, can be said to have achieved its objectives in Vukovar to the extent that the Serbians had designated Vukovar to be the capital of the proclaimed Serbian autonomous region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem. Therefore, albeit a destroyed city, they had captured the city which they designated would be the capital of this town. From the JNA perspective, they had secured a territory in Eastern Slavonia, including Vukovar, which would be a Serbian territory and would, therefore, achieve one of the primary objectives of the JNA, according to General Kadijevic, which was to protect the Serbian population, to give them areas in which they would be in control. The JNA, I think, did not achieve its objective of creating the spring board for an offensive through Slavonia towards Zagreb because of the defections from the conscript cadre and because of developments in the international environment. I think that is something that they would acknowledge but, in terms of securing control of Vukovar, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they secure control of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vukovar was surrendered by Croatian forces on 18th November 1981. 7 MR. NIEMANN: Your Honours, I have no further questions of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, prosecuting counsel. I would now like to address my judge colleagues, madam? JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you. Dr. Gow, could you tell the Tribunal what happened with the Muslim community during the Second World War and in the aftermath of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If your Honour is asking me about the Muslim communities in the whole of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in the whole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, some of the Muslims in the early stages certainly sided with the Ustasha regime and with the Axis powers and the SS Handzar division was primarily composed of these Muslim volunteers. On the other side, in other parts of Bosnia and many Muslims, there were thousands of Muslims massacred by the Serbian Chetniks with the result that there were different patterns within the Muslim population in Bosnia and in the Sandzak, some of them joining with the partisans, some of them for periods siding with the Axis powers in this way. This gave rise to some problems in Bosnia, some of which, I think, continued after the war. In particular, there were also questions with relation to the war in the context of discussing war crimes alleged to have been committed in the context of the war in Croatia in 1991. The impact on Croatia in the Bihac area was such that there were problems -- the Muslims in that area were judged as being highly volatile as a population group, and there was a suggestion at one stage, but always linked with Croatia, and there was a suggestion at the end of the war by the People's Republic of Bosnia that the Bihac area should be transferred to Croatia. That did not happen. I hope that is a satisfactory answer; if not, I am happy to elaborate. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to ask you a few questions in the light of this extremely interesting historical background you gave us. I gathered from what you said that the Ustashas and the responsible Croats declared that they are planning to kill, and I quote, "one out of three Serbs or convert them to the orthodox creed". How far was this applied? Was it applied only to the Serbs or also to the Serbs and to the Bosniac Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The programme was put into effect and it is clear that a large number of Serbs were killed. The number of Serbs killed is a subject of great dispute. I think in my testimony I alluded to the fact that one of the features of post 1945 Yugoslavia, Tito's communist Yugoslavia, was that many of the events of the Second World War were not properly accounted, and in this context the precise number of Serbs who were killed either in the war as a whole or as a result of the Ustasha programme is hard to fix. It is fair to say that it was a large number who were killed. Further than that, a large number were expelled from Croatian controlled territory, but many remained and many remained fighting either in smaller groups with Chetnik forces or predominantly with the partisans. The Ustasha was not exclusively designed to eliminate Serbs, although the Serbs were the largest group in Croatia and became a primary focus of that activity. The camps that were established by the Ustasha, some of which were death camps, also included anti-Ustasha Croats, included communists, included Jews, included some people of other groupings but they were predominantly -- the predominant group taken into the camps were Serbs. The Bosniac Muslims, some were aligned with the Ustasha regime, as I said, fighting with the SS Handzar division; others were opposed to the Croatian Ustasha regime. I should clarify, if it was not clear either from the map or my testimony before, that the independent state of Croatia, the Ustasha state, embraced large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the main part of Croatia and Slavonia. There were areas in which the Ustasha was turned against the Muslims primarily because the Muslims were siding with the partisans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you assimilate this attitude with the idea of racial cleansing, ethnic cleansing, and consider that this was the outbreak of ethnic cleansing in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- I think we would have to -- we probably need to have a seminar discussing the exact meaning of ethnic cleansing. Some people have said the term should apply to the arrangement between Greece and Turkey over Anatolia in which there was a peaceful exchange of populations because the territory was purified. In contemporary terms, I think the label "ethnic cleansing" is associated with the forcible expulsion, if not probably including demonstrative killing, of certain population groups. In that context, I think it is certainly fair to say that the Ustasha programme with systematic elements, including camps, was a manifestation of an ethnic cleansing programme and one which in many ways, it could be argued, those involved in the Serbian side in the 1990s were mimicking. I have even seen indications that the term "ethnic cleansing" was used in Croatian documents at the time, but I have not seen the original documents and cannot be sure that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question, you mentioned that the JNA was involved in Vukovar's assault. Is there any indication that they had orders from their higher command or was it just on the spur of the moment that they acted this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be very difficult to imagine that this was a spontaneous action. I think any experienced military man would tell you that you are not able to organise several different units, even within one military district, let alone bringing units from another military district, as a spontaneous action, and then to position those forces almost completely encircling a town and keep it under siege and then keep it for a period of three months and keep that force supplied. I, therefore, would take it as a matter of deduction that to have that size of force deployed in such a way cannot in any sense be conceived of as a spontaneous action. In addition to that, I would say, just before your Honours began your questions, I indicated that there were two operational groups in the area involving the sets of forces deployed by the JNA, one under the command of General Biorcevi}, the other under the command of Colonel Mile Mrk{i}. That in itself, I think, indicates that there was significant JNA control of what was going on in that situation at the time. I would further add that I believe that there is, that there was film evidence shown on radio television Belgrade of the various commanders, not only General Biorcevi} and Colonel Mile Mrk{i}, but also of the commander of the 1st Military District, General Zivota Panic, who was later to become the Secretary, the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav army -- that is of the successor Yugoslav army, not the JNA, but the Vojska Juglosvaije of the current Serbia Montenegro; he is now out of office -- General Panic who was then commander of the 1st Military District, along with General Biorcevi} and Colonel Mile Mrk{i} was being congratulated by the then Federal Defence Secretary, General Kadijevic, and his deputy and Chief of Staff, General Adzic, following the collapse of Vukovar. So, I think all this indicates that there could be little doubt that it was a JNA operation; that it could not have been spontaneous and that it was organised and approved by the JNA command mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or by the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would anticipate that it has to have been approved by the political leadership. I would say that the evidence indicates that it cannot have taken place without organisation and without organisation and orders from the military command structures. I have little doubt in my own mind that it was organised with political -- that it was approved and authorised by political authorities as well. Some indication of this can be found, I suspect, in the memoirs of the Croatian representative to the federal presidency in the final stage of Yugoslavia, Stipe Mesic, who in many instances makes reference to the way in which General Kadijevic was formally taking orders from the Montenegrin representative, Mr. Kostic, as the representing the rump presidency of the SFRY, as they alleged it still was at the time. They were trying to argue that the SFRY continued and that the four representatives continuing to form a body on the presidency, the representative of Serbia, the representative of Montenegro and of the two Serbian provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina, were said to provide the leadership and Mr. Kostic was giving the instructions to General Kadijevic at least on a formal level. So, in that sense, I think, there was a political -- there was certainly some political level of instruction and command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just ask you my last question: You indicated the importance of Vukovar for the Serbian part. In the light of this importance, in your assessment, what would have been the ultimate goal of the assault of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The primary Serbian goal, I would judge, was to occupy Vukovar and to drive out the non-Serbian, the non-loyal population in an example of a practice of which we see many examples afterwards in Croatia, but particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the practice generally called ethnic cleansing. I think the purpose was to drive out the civilian population to be able to take control of the area to form the border of the territory which was to be part of the Republika Srpska Krajina, that is, the territory of the previously declared Serbian autonomous region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem. I think the evidence would indicate that that was the case. The purpose was to create a territory for the Serbian people, to make Vukovar part of that territory and to remove the non-Serbian population. For the JNA, there was a secondary purpose, that it would then be the launching pad for attacks through Western Slavonia to Zagreb, but that was an option, the second phase of the JNA operations, which never came into effect. So, in Serbian JNA terms, the first priority was to get rid of the population and to make the town, in whatever condition, part of that territory under Serbian control. The second option was only for the JNA and was one which I think the Serbian communities did not support sufficiently to make it possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, just to add to the questions which were already asked, can you confirm that there was actually a concerted plan, a systematic attack on Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can confirm that there were forces of the JNA and in addition, Serbian paramilitary or volunteer forces which were deployed to encircle Vukovar as a town; that a deployment of that kind could not have taken place without planning and without organisation from command structures. I would also confirm that, according to the then Federal Secretary for Defence, General Kadijevic, that the object was to provide an area for the Serbian people and that the Vukovar would be a key element of that territory and that, therefore, Vukovar and the area in Eastern Slavonia was seen as being an important aspect of the first phase of the plan which the JNA had for operations in the second half of 1991, that is, the project to create borders of new territories which would be part of what they saw was a continuing federal mini Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also confirm that there are also written records or radiophonic records of declarations, statements made by superiors, people in charge, people who are currently the object of this indictment, who expressed their satisfaction with the success of the attack on Vukovar? Can you confirm your references you gave concerning these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can confirm that there was televisual evidence of the Federal Secretary for Defence, General Kadijevic, and his deputy, General Adzic, congratulating the commander of the 1st Military District, General Panic, and the commanders of the two operational groups, Colonel Mile Mrk{i} and General Biorcevi}, following the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More generally speaking, Mr. Gow, what was the attitude of the major western powers around 1991, that is, about the time of the declaration of independence? How would you characterise this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. That is a very big question. I think the international environment in which the declarations of independence occurred, and in which the dissolution of Yugoslavia took place, was one which was in a state, which characterised by a state of flux. It was one which was broadly reluctant to see the dissolution of Yugoslavia or of any other federal state at that stage take place, particularly because Yugoslavia was seen as a small version of what might happen and, indeed, eventually did happen in the Soviet Union. There were different perspectives from different countries within Europe and within the international community broadly, but I would say that the majority of states at the time we are talking about were in a process of moving from being either opposed to or reluctant to see the dissolution of Yugoslavia to a position where they recognised that the dissolution was to all intents and purposes inevitable. This was seen through, I think, the framework of the European Community Conference organised under the chair of Lord Carrington here in The Hague, where there were attempts made to try to preserve a Yugoslav framework for the various Yugoslav states, but I think, in general, in a six month period where everybody was moving towards the recognition that at some stage the dissolution of Yugoslavia would have to be accepted and most of the arguments were coming to be about the timing when that should be accepted as a fact. I hope that is an adequate answer. I am happy to elaborate if you have more specific questions, or if you feel that I should elaborate generally?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was relatively simple; it was just whether the major powers, when they supported independence, did they encourage or favour movements towards Serbism, Croatism or were they more cautious in their attitude? Were they more cautious with regard to respect of cultural or religious entities? Do you, as an expert, believe that maybe they were playing with fire a bit, or do you think that, basically, this was just part of a destiny of the Balkans as you have been describing it for the last 100 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think inevitably in some sense they were playing with fire because there was a war taking place, and it was a difficult and dangerous situation both in terms of the armed conflict and in terms of the issues of international order that were being put into a framework of questions at that time. I think the work of the European Community conference under the presidency of the French constitutional -- the President of the French constitutional court, Monsieur Badinter, went some way towards clarifying some of the issues involved and made it easier for the international community and particularly for the European Community (as it then was) to understand the processes in ways which it could accommodate, to look to the process, to say that, for example, it would no longer be possible to sustain a joint state comprising the various republics, but that it should be possible to try to sustain some kind of future for the federating elements, for the republics defined as states and with the quality of sovereignty. In that context, I think most states were, essentially, cautious. It is broadly recognised that Austria and Germany, Austria before the declarations of independence and Germany fairly quickly afterwards, certainly by 24th August, was very much open to the possibility of accepting the break up of Yugoslavia and recognising the independence of the republics. It is also said at the other extreme that France and Spain until a very late stage at the end of the year were reluctant to see the breakup take place. This may reflect cultural differences. In the case of France, it has a highly centralised system of government, whereas Germany has a highly decentralised federal system of government, maybe has a different understanding of situations. In the case of France, I could speculate that because -- sorry, in the case of Spain, I could speculate that because Spain has been said to have a number of questions of its own, perhaps with Catalonia, perhaps with the Basque country, that Spain was reluctant to see processes of this kind. I think the Badinter Commission was important because it clarified a number of the issues involved and made it easier for the states of the European Community, in the first instance, to accept the break up of Yugoslavia in terms of statehood and borders in a way which would not have implications, for example, in the Spanish case for Basque territories or Catalonia. Between that, I think the majority of states were extremely cautious. They were in a difficult situation and it was a time of transition. Many eyes were focused on the Soviet Union and events there. Many eyes had been focused on events in the Middle East. There had been the Gulf conflict at the end of 1990 and in the first part of 1991. It was one question among many, and it was a very, very difficult question, one which states gradually and cautiously came to accept in a particular -- they gradually and cautiously came to accept a particular interpretation of that. The interpretation sometimes led some countries to be characterised as proSerb and some countries to be characterised as pro-Croat during the war in Croatia. I am not sure to what extent it is useful, if we are being serious, to try to have a kind of understanding of what was going on in those terms. I think the realities in the foreign ministries of all these countries were very different to the simple labelling of pro-Croat or proSerb or anything else of that kind. In that context, I think I would just finish, I would say that the major issue -- as I understand it, the major issue by the end of 1991 was not recognising the independence of those republics seeking it, but on the time of recognition and on the need to establish an overall framework of mutual agreements before that was accepted, and that was the source of a big dispute within the European community between Germany and Denmark, I think, on one hand and a number of other countries at the end of 1991 in December. I hope that has been helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you another question, Mr. Gow. With regard to the militia, you mentioned armed militia, you quoted names. In your studies you know this region very well. Do these militia remain constituted for a long time after the events in Vukovar? What happened to these militia after -- do they still exist secretly? What happened afterwards? They seem to have played a very important role.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an extremely difficult question to answer. By militia or paramilitary group, we can understand some different phenomena. The groups organised in the Kninska/Krajina area were, essentially, local Serbs. There may have been Serbs from other places, but it was based around the idea of a local Serbian identity, and they were using the structures of the old territorial defence system. As you are aware, I should -- as you may well be aware, last August Croatian forces attacked the Krajina area and the Serbian forces were retreated and driven out, so now they no longer exist in those areas. The paramilitary groups, some of which I mentioned in the Vukovar area, such as Arkan's Tigers, are not known to be present in many or any areas, to my knowledge, at the moment. Whether this means that they no longer exist, I would hesitate to say. I suspect it is in the nature of these groups that the people who organise them would very quickly arrange for the groups to be together and present in any situation where the groups' leaders or where the political authorities to whom they might be connected would say that they would be needed, but I think at the moment they are not a group -- that these groups are not a significant feature at the moment other than by their absence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you Dr. Gow. I think that is the end of the questions, the end of The Prosecutor's questions and those from the Tribunal. Dr. Gow, the Tribunal would like to thank you for your contribution do its work concerning this affair, concerning the attack on Vukovar. We thank you sincerely. I think you are free now. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This time, your Honours, we would like to call Dennis Milner as the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could the usher please bring in Mr. Dennis Milner? Thank you. MR. DENNIS MILNER, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dennis Milner, you are going to make the declaration. You have the text. Maybe you could give Mr. Denis Milner the head set?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I shall speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you do not mind, Mr. Milner, could you put the head set on, thank you, so that the presiding judge is sure that you hear everything. Do you hear me OK? 1 THE WITNESS: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So please make your declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. I am Dennis James Milner. I am a Detective Inspector from the United Kingdom police service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please be seated? Prosecuting Counsel, you have the floor for your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Milner, you indicated that you are a Police Officer from the United Kingdom. Could you inform the court how long you have been so employed? 2 A. Yes, I have been a Police Officer for in excess of 26 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am currently seconded from the British Government to the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of work do you do at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am engaged in investigating events in former Yugoslavia during the period from 1991 through to the present day, but, in particular, I have been engaged with my immediate colleagues in investigating events in the area of Croatia and Eastern Slavonia, in particular, during 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been involved in the investigation of events which occurred in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was seconded to the International Tribunal on 1st May 1995, and since that time I have been engaged in investigations relating solely to Vukovar and the Vukovar area. 1 Q. OK. During this period and during the course of your investigation, have you become familiar with events which occurred there during the year of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I obtained my knowledge through research of documents that have been written, through news media articles, through witness statements, the reading of witness statements taken by government and non-government organisations, and by interviewing of witnesses personally, and the liaison with my immediate colleagues who have also been engaged in interviewing witnesses and victims and the reading of their statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this way have you become familiar with the information that has been provided by these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point during the year 1991, are you aware of the JNA becoming actively involved in the conflict which was ongoing in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what was the role of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role of the JNA, as far as my knowledge goes (and it is not as extensive as the previous witness, obviously), but the role of the JNA at that time appeared to be more as a mediator between the warring factions of the Croatians and Serbians who had set up small groups of villages who were squabbling and having petty disputes between themselves. When I say "petty", I mean petty in terms of the overall situation within the war in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time were you aware of the role of the JNA changing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did it change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the late summer of 1991, there was a time when many of the ethnic Croatians who had been conscripted to the JNA and people from other countries had started deserting in quite large numbers, and it was clear that the JNA had taken on the role of arming some of the paramilitary units and what were referred to as Serb irregular groups, the volunteer groups from many of the villages in Eastern Slavonia. The JNA would actively support the actions and supply armaments to these particular groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time did this action by the JNA escalate into active involvement in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Certainly, during July and through August of 1991, really culminating around August 29th 1991, siege had been laid to Vukovar by a large number of troops, a large amount of artillery, air force and naval units, jointly with some of the paramilitary units from that area and surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of activities did these units engage in regarding their attack on Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 29th August, Vukovar was being subjected to constant bombardment, shelling, bombings by aircraft; so much so that people living within Vukovar had to resort to living in shelters for fear of being killed, and by that time a large number had already been killed as a result of the military action in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These bombardments you have referred to, how long did these go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the bombardments continued through August, September, October, right up until the actual fall of the city of Vukovar on 18th November when the Croatian soldiers and defenders, what was left of them, really had no choice but to surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over that three month period what was the result of the bombardments on the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
